title: Research Bite #34: Noise, Cognitive Function, and Worker Productivity
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #34 summarizes Joshua T. Dean's study on noise, cognitive function, and worker productivity, which provides some of the first causal, real-world evidence that ambient noise impairs cognitive performance and output. Working with textile factory laborers in Kenya, Dean found that a 10-decibel increase in noise (roughly the jump from a dishwasher to a vacuum cleaner) measurably reduced productivity, and that this effect was driven specifically by impaired cognitive function — attention and working memory — rather than by reduced effort. Strikingly, workers' willingness to pay for quieter conditions did not change based on whether their pay depended on performance, suggesting they were largely unaware of how much noise was costing them. Barton's classroom translation is direct: students in noisy environments may be losing attention and working-memory capacity without realizing it, and simply expecting them to adapt is unlikely to work. The paper argues this points toward active intervention — physical noise reduction or explicit awareness-raising — rather than assuming students will self-correct.
points: A 10 dB increase in background noise measurably reduced worker output by impairing cognitive function (attention, working memory), not by reducing effort — a mechanism directly relevant to noisy classrooms and open-plan learning spaces.

Workers' willingness to pay for quiet conditions did not track whether their pay depended on performance, suggesting people are largely unaware of how much noise is degrading their own output — a caution against assuming students will notice and self-correct.

Because the underlying data come from a sewing task and engine noise in a Kenyan factory, teachers should treat the classroom implications as a reasonable extrapolation, not a direct classroom finding.
The finding reframes noise pollution as a hidden equity issue: cognitive impairment from noise appears to hit hardest precisely when people can't detect or price the harm themselves.
quotes: This document explores the impact of noise on worker productivity in a real-world setting.
Through experiments with textile workers, it demonstrates that increased noise levels reduce output, suggesting that noise significantly impairs cognitive function, which is crucial for such tasks.

Noise can impair cognitive functions, such as attention and working memory, which are crucial for task management and performance, and individuals (like the workers in this study) may not be aware of how significantly noise affects their performance
Excessive noise can significantly impair students' cognitive functions, such as attention and working memory, which are crucial for learning and academic success.
The research found that even a 10 dB increase in noise (equivalent to moving from a dishwasher to a vacuum cleaner's sound) reduces performance.
This cautions against the ability of workers to appropriately adapt to the impacts of noise and suggests dealing with environmental cognitive impediments may require policy intervention
